title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives & Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
summary: Standardized SRE guidance for defining SLOs and error budgets, running capacity planning, coordinating reliability initiatives, conducting incident reviews, and authoring/runbook maintenance.
body:
Purpose

This page defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards across: SLO and error budget definitions, capacity planning cadence, reliability initiatives (RCA/mitigation lifecycle), incident review expectations, operational tooling recommendations, and runbook templates. The goal is to create consistent, measurable, and reproducible practices that reduce outage risk and speed recovery.

Scope

Applies to all production services managed by the SRE organization and service owners that have customer-facing SLAs or internal latency/throughput SLOs (Redwood API, routing services, dedicated serving clusters, private deployment control plane).

1) SLO & Error Budget Standards

- SLO types (recommended):
  - Availability (successful user-facing requests) — primary for outward-facing APIs.
  - Latency (p99, p95, p50 depending on feature) — use p95 for business flows, p99 for critical synchronous paths.
  - Correctness/Quality (inference quality regressions, evaluation-driven checks) — measured via periodic evals/metric hooks.

- Minimum SLO definition fields (required in each service SLO doc):
  1. SLO name (short): e.g. "API request availability"
  2. Objective: e.g. "99.95% success over 30-day rolling window"
  3. Measurement method: data source (edge LB logs / telemetry pipeline), success criteria, and aggregation window
  4. Burndown window for error budget: daily and 30-day burn rate dashboards
  5. Owner: service owner and oncall rotation
  6. Exemptions: planned maintenance, data migrations, controlled experiments (must be pre-notified)

- Error budget policy (standard):
  - Error budget = 1 - SLO objective. Track 30-day rolling burn and 7-day short-term burn.
  - If 7-day burn rate > 3x expected -> service-level action required (see Remediation & Escalation).
  - If 30-day budget exhausted -> immediate halt on non-essential launches and feature rollouts, mandatory postmortem for budget burn, and dedicated reliability initiative until budget is positive.

- Alerting & Dashboards:
  - Required dashboards: SLO overview (objective, current attainment, 30-day trend), burn rate chart, recent incidents contributing to burn, top error types.
  - Required alerts: 7-day burn > 2x expected (warning), 7-day burn > 3x expected (actionable), 30-day budget < 10% remaining (pre-emptive). Alerts should route to SRE oncall and service owner.

2) Capacity Planning Standards

Cadence and responsibilities:
- Quarterly capacity review owned jointly by SRE and service/product owners.
- Monthly capacity health check (automated) reporting: utilization, headroom, queue depth, throttling events, KV-cache hit rates.

Inputs and outputs:
- Inputs: traffic forecasts (product), historical telemetry (30/90/180 day), new feature resource estimates, cloud pricing/availability windows, contractual commitments (Dedicated capacity).
- Outputs: scaling runway (weeks), allocation requests (GPU types and counts), autoscaler policy changes, runway mitigation playbook (burst-capacity purchase plan, rate-limiting policy changes).

Capacity thresholds and SLO interplay:
- Define headroom targets per service tier:
  - Tier-1 (critical): maintain 40% spare serving capacity at expected peak
  - Tier-2 (important): maintain 25% spare capacity
  - Tier-3 (non-critical / experimental): maintain 10% spare capacity
- If capacity alarms triggered (e.g., utilization > 70% sustained for 10m at p95), route to runbook for autoscaler/rebalance.

Capacity runbook quick checklist:
1. Validate telemetry (ingest lag, aggregation errors).
2. Identify hot services and allocation gaps.
3. Apply short-term mitigations: rate limit, degrade non-critical features, enable burst pools.
4. Submit provisioning request or schedule capacity increases per procurement SLA.

3) Reliability Initiatives & Roadmap Integration

- Initiatives: prioritized from top SLA-impacting failure modes (from incident reviews and metric regressions). Examples: KV-cache hardening, dynamic batching improvements, model warm cache persistence, HA control plane for private customers.
- Initiative lifecycle:
  1. Problem statement & target metric (owner + sponsor).
  2. Baseline measurement and ROI estimate (reduced outage minutes, cost savings per month).
  3. Implementation plan with milestones (canary, A/B, rollback criteria).
  4. Evaluation: post-deploy SLO delta and regression tests.
  5. Close with updated runbooks and monitoring updates.

Governance:
- SRE quarterly reliability review with product leadership to approve top initiatives and budget resourcing.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortem & RCA)

- When to run a postmortem: any incident that breaches an SLO, exhausts error budget, or causes customer-visible degradation > 15 minutes.

- Postmortem structure (required fields):
  - Incident ID and timeline (UTC): detection -> mitigation -> recovery -> full resolution
  - Severity and SLO impact (quantified minutes or % points)
  - Root causes (technical and process) and contributing factors
  - Immediate remediation steps taken and rationale
  - Corrective action plan with owners and due dates (small, medium, large buckets)
  - Verification plan and how SLO/metrics will be validated post-fix
  - Lessons learned and knowledge artifacts added to runbooks

- Review cadence: postmortems must be published within 3 business days of incident resolution and reviewed at SRE weekly review. High-severity incidents should have a dedicated 1:1 review with a senior engineering reviewer within 7 days.

- Blamelessness: Focus on systems and process fixes. Signal-to-noise: include signal artifacts (logs, traces, config diffs) to make reviews factual and actionable.

5) Operational Tooling Recommendations

Required tooling stack (minimum):
- Telemetry: centralized metrics (Prometheus / Cortex), traces (Jaeger/Tempo), logs (ELK or Loki) integrated into a single SRE dashboard.
- Alerting: PagerDuty for oncall rotation, Opsgenie or built-in comms for lower-severity routing.
- SLO management: Grafana SLOs / custom SLO pipeline with automated burn rate alerts.
- Capacity & cost: cloud billing export, cluster autoscaler metrics, GPU fleet dashboard.
- Runbook/Playbook storage: Confluence for canonical runbooks + Git repo for runnable automation and scripts.

Operational integrations required for new services:
- SRE onboarding checklist (required): metrics emitted, alert oncall configured, SLO defined & reviewed, runbook authored, ownership added to roster.

6) Runbook Template & Maintenance

- Runbook sections (required):
  1. Service Overview: one-paragraph summary, critical paths, owners, contact info.
  2. SLOs & Key Metrics: link to SLO doc and embed critical thresholds.
  3. Symptoms: how user-facing issues manifest (errors, latency, throttling).
  4. Detection: dashboards and alerts that indicate this problem.
  5. Impact Assessment: quick checklist to estimate customer impact.
  6. Immediate Mitigations (step-by-step): numbered commands and CLI examples.
  7. Root Cause Drilldown steps: how to collect logs/traces and common failure modes.
  8. Recovery & Rollback: explicit steps for rollforward and rollback with safe checks.
  9. Post-Incident Actions: tasks to implement in follow-up (owner + due date).
  10. References: runbooks, dashboards, config files, and related postmortems.

- Example runbook snippet (CLI examples):
  - Check queue depth:
    kubectl -n serving get hpa my-service -o yaml  # inspect autoscaler
    curl -sS "https://metrics.internal/api/series?query=serving_queue_depth%7Bservice=\"my-service\"%7D" | jq .
  - Enable degraded mode (route to fallback):
    curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://ops-api.internal/v1/route-degrade -d '{"service":"my-service","mode":"fallback"}'

- Runbook ownership & review policy:
  - Service owners must review runbooks quarterly or after any related incident.
  - SRE triage will audit runbooks for top-20 services monthly. Missing or stale runbooks escalate to owner.

7) Remediation & Escalation Matrix

- Standard escalation path:
  1. Primary oncall (SRE) -> 2. Service owner -> 3. SRE lead -> 4. Engineering manager -> 5. CTO (for customer-impacting SEV1).
- Escalation triggers: SLO breach lasting > 15 minutes, error budget > 100% burn in rolling 24 hours, security incident affecting production.

8) Operationalizing the Standards (how to adopt)

- Onboarding checklist for new service owners (must be completed before production acceptance):
  - Create SLO doc and publish in Confluence
  - Configure SLO dashboards and burn alerts
  - Author initial runbook and attach to service Confluence page
  - Add owners to oncall rotation and PagerDuty
  - Complete a tabletop exercise simulated outage with SRE

- Rolling adoption plan (recommended):
  - Phase 1 (30 days): top-10 revenue-impact services complete full checklist
  - Phase 2 (90 days): all Tier-1/Tier-2 services completed
  - Phase 3 (180 days): audit and automated compliance checks in CI for new services

Appendix: Example SLO table (template)

| SLO name | Objective | Measurement source | Window | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---|
| API availability | 99.95% | edge-lb success rate | 30d | @serving-team | Excludes scheduled maintenance |
| Chat latency (p95) | < 450ms | request latency pipeline | 30d | @runtime-team | p99 target set separately for critical flows |

How to contribute

If you are a service owner or SRE and need to propose an update, create a PR against this Confluence page draft in the docs repo and request review from the SRE lead. For urgent changes post-incident, update the page immediately and add a follow-up PR with rationale.
